title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade
oneLiner: Dwellings built per new resident have fallen, and vacancy rates in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth sit near record lows.
body: Completions peaked around 2017 and fell through the pandemic as costs rose and builders failed, while population growth resumed at pace. The national housing agency's projections show a cumulative shortfall against household formation through the second half of the decade.
contextBackground: This claim sits underneath several debates at once: migration, negative gearing, planning and parking all argue about the causes and cures of the same shortfall. It is written once here so each debate connects to the same evidence.
contextDisagreement: The shortfall is broadly accepted. What is contested is how much of it reflects demand growth and how much reflects construction capacity, planning constraints and financing, because each answer points to a different policy.

otherClaim.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes

claimItself.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes
claimItself.oneLiner: The policy is now a bill before the Senate: negative gearing for new builds only from July 2027, existing investors grandfathered, and a reworked capital gains discount alongside it.
claimItself.body: The 12 May 2026 budget restricted negative gearing to newly built residential property for investments made after budget night, with effect from 1 July 2027, and replaced the 50 per cent capital gains discount with an inflation-based discount and a 30 per cent floor. Anyone using the concessions before budget night keeps them. A Senate inquiry took evidence in June 2026.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: The large majority of investor housing loans finance established dwellings rather than new construction

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Limiting negative gearing to new builds would make housing materially more affordable

otherClaim.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year

claimItself.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the federal government should cap net arrivals below the levels of the past decade and well below the post-pandemic peak.
claimItself.body: Net overseas migration is arrivals minus departures of people who stay, or leave, for at least twelve months. It averaged just over 200,000 a year in the decade before the pandemic and exceeded 500,000 in 2022–23. The proposal is a cap of 200,000, which would require the government to manage the student, temporary-work and permanent programs together to hit it.

otherClaim.title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing

claimItself.title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether planning schemes should stop requiring a set number of car spaces per new dwelling and let builders decide.
claimItself.body: Most Australian planning schemes require new apartments and townhouses to include a minimum number of off-street car spaces, typically one or more per dwelling. The proposal removes the minimum. Developers could still build parking; they would no longer be required to.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Parking minimums add roughly $70,000 to the cost of a two-bedroom apartment in Sydney, $62,000 in Melbourne and up to $137,000 in Perth

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Auckland removed minimum parking requirements citywide in 2016, and new developments near frequent transit have since provided markedly less parking

otherClaim.title: The 2020 independent review of the EPBC Act found its approval processes slow, duplicative and unpredictable

claimItself.title: The 2020 independent review of the EPBC Act found its approval processes slow, duplicative and unpredictable
claimItself.oneLiner: The government's own review reached the conclusion industry had been making for years.
claimItself.body: The review, led by Professor Graeme Samuel, found that assessment and approval under the Act duplicated state processes, took far longer than the statutory timeframes suggested, and gave proponents little certainty about what would be required of them.

claimItself.title: Net overseas migration in 2022–23 was roughly double the average of the decade before the pandemic
claimItself.oneLiner: The post-pandemic intake was far above any previous year.
claimItself.body: The Bureau of Statistics recorded net overseas migration above 500,000 in 2022–23, against an average of a little over 200,000 a year across 2010 to 2019. It was the largest annual intake on record by a wide margin.
